title: Tumble's Crumble Calamity
markdown:
The old museum room was usually a quiet place, hushed whispers and gentle echoes from long ago. Sunlight, warm and mellow like honey, streamed through the tall arched windows and lit dust motes that danced as if they had been invited. Asha, the museum helper, moved with a quiet grace, her cloth gliding over a case of whisper-thin teacups whose painted flowers seemed caught in eternal bloom.

A worried sigh drifted toward her, dry leaves on a small wind. It came from Tumble, the museum’s resident goat. His woolly coat, usually cheerful, drooped with concern.

“Asha,” he bleated, hazelnut eyes wide. “The Harvest Festival is tomorrow. Professor Imani’s Enchanted Apple Crumble — the amounts are smudged.”

Asha’s steps were as soft as falling leaves. Tumble nudged a parchment with a damp nose. Where flour, sugar, and butter should have stood in neat lines, the ink had become a messy blur.

“It says something like a whole cup of apples,” Asha murmured, tracing a faint line. “The flour looks like a half cup. The sugar… maybe three eighths? And the butter is almost gone.”

Tumble made a little munch-munch and looked at the floor. “I only tasted a tiny bit. Now we won’t have crumble.”

The worry settled, a quiet blanket in the sun-dappled room.

The heavy door creaked. Golden light chased a few shadows. Professor Imani stepped in, smile warm as a hearth, eyes bright. She took in the smudged recipe, Tumble’s apologetic posture, Asha’s frown. She did not scold. From her woven basket she drew a perfectly round apple, blush of red and gold.

“Consider this.” A small polished knife. She sliced the apple down the centre into two equal pieces. “Two the same. Halves.” She held one up, then cut that half again. Four neat quarters on the clean wooden table. One quarter divided once more. “Eighths.” She lined them up so Tumble could see the family: one apple, two halves, four quarters, eight small boats of pale flesh.

Tumble watched, mesmerized. His usual boisterous chewing slowed. He counted under his breath, which for a goat sounded like a polite nibble. He nudged a fallen papery leaf toward Asha, as if the garden had offered another example and he did not want to waste it. Asha folded the leaf once, then again, and the creases made the same story without juice.

Asha looked at the parchment, then at Tumble, who was now gently herding a small accidental pile of spilled flour with his nose. “If we know what a whole looks like, we can make halves, and quarters, and eighths.”

She found a clean bowl and a clear measuring cup. “Butter first. It looks like a half cup.” She filled the cup, found the halfway mark, and scooped out precisely half, leaving the rest in the tub. Tumble nudged a pile of glistening sugar toward the bowl.

“Three eighths for sugar?” Asha whispered. She filled the cup, pictured Imani’s eighths on the table, divided the white hill into eight equal parts with the edge of the spoon, and added three. Two parts stayed behind like unused snow. For flour the smudge looked like a quarter. Steady hands poured just that, and Tumble watched the cup as if it might try to become a half when no one was looking.

They peeled the apples last, the one whole cup that had survived the smudge, and tipped the slices into the bowl. Butter, sugar, flour, fruit: a quiet argument that smelled like winning. Asha scraped the bowl with a wooden spoon that knew the museum kitchen better than the display cases did.

A sweet scent began to weave through the quiet rooms: baked apple, butter, sugar, flour. It found the teacups and made them look suddenly decorative. The crumble went into the oven. Tumble sat with unusual patience, only once stretching his neck toward the door as if the festival had arrived early. When the dish came out golden-brown, his tail gave a little wag. “It’s beautiful.”

Imani smiled and left the oaks to their own weather. She cut a small tasting square for Tumble, who had already paid in smudges, and a neater one for Asha. Steam rose. Tumble closed his eyes for the first bite, which was, Asha thought, as close as a goat came to taking notes.

Asha copied the amounts onto a fresh card while the crumble was still warm enough to perfume the ink: apples, 1 cup; butter, 1/2; sugar, 3/8; flour, 1/4. She pinned it inside the recipe tin so a goat’s curiosity would have to work harder next time.

Moonlight began to stretch sleepy shadows across the floor. The scent of apples made the room feel finished. Asha yawned into her smile. Tumble rested his woolly head on the cool stone, eyes drifting toward dreams that, for once, did not include extra butter. The teacups kept their eternal bloom. The festival, in the morning, would have a crumble that could be measured twice.
